metadata.title: Accelerated Approval and Considerations for Determining Whether a Confirmatory Trial is Underway
metadata.topic: Draft guideline · FDA human drugs and biologics

candidates.statement: 6 For purposes of section 506(c), FDA interprets the term “study” to include a clinical investigation such as a randomized, controlled trial, which is the type of confirmatory study that is typically required to confirm benefit, as well as other types of studies. In this guidance, references to a confirmatory “trial” or “study” should be understood to mean one or more trials or studies, as appropriate for the relevant product. The terms trials and studies are used interchangeably in this guidance. Policies regarding studies other than those that may be required under section 506(c) are beyond the scope of this guidance. Sponsors are encouraged to discuss with FDA early in the development process what studies should be conducted to verify and confirm benefit, and conditions for any such studies. The fact that this guidance refers to clinical trials as a type of clinical study should not be read to suggest that FDA considers clinical trials to be studies under section 505(o) of the FD&C Act, which authorizes FDA under specific conditions to require postapproval clinical trials and studies.
candidates.context: 5 Section 506(c)(2)(D) of the FD&C Act; Pub. L. No. 117-328. 7 The terms postapproval , postmarketing , and confirmatory are used interchangeably throughout this guidance to describe the postapproval studies that FDA requires under section 506(c) of the FD&C Act. 21 CFR 314.510 refers to these postapproval studies as postmarketing studies , and the term confirmatory studies has commonly been used to describe studies that are completed postapproval and are intended to verify clinical benefit.

candidates.statement: Sponsors have therefore been required to conduct postapproval trials to verify clinical benefit of 95 drugs granted accelerated approval. These confirmatory studies protect the public health and the 96 integrity of the drug approval process by balancing earlier approval of drugs with an assurance 97 that studies will be conducted to resolve residual uncertainty about benefit. Confirmatory trials 98 must be completed with due diligence. 9 It is critical that such studies are promptly initiated and 99 completed in a timely manner to limit the time that a drug is approved for an indication without 100 verification of clinical benefit. This is especially important when the drug has considerable 101 toxicity because the longer the time between approval and verification of clinical benefit the 102 more patients will be exposed to the toxicity without verification of clinical benefit. 103
candidates.context: receiving traditional approval, which may mean there is less information about the occurrence of 92 rare or delayed adverse events. 93 While many confirmatory trials are completed in a timely fashion, some have been slow to 105 initiate or have stalled, resulting in long delays or even uncertainty about whether studies can be 106 completed. In the Consolidated Appropriations Act, Congress provided FDA with additional 107 authorities to help prevent such delays, including that FDA may, when appropriate, require a 108 confirmatory study or studies to be underway prior to approval. 9

candidates.statement: Randomized controlled trials are commonly required to verify clinical benefit of a drug granted 115 accelerated approval and may be challenging to conduct (especially placebo-controlled studies) 116 if the trial is not underway when the drug is approved. For drug development programs intending 117 to seek accelerated approval, FDA generally intends to require that the confirmatory trial(s) be 118 underway prior to the accelerated approval action. 10 If FDA determines that a confirmatory trial 119 must be underway prior to accelerated approval and the trial is not underway, FDA does not 120 intend to grant accelerated approval until this deficiency is addressed. 11 In some cases, when 121 FDA determines that continued enrollment/retention after the drug product is on the market is 122 likely to be especially challenging, FDA may require enrollment to be complete at the time of 123 approval. 124
candidates.context: III. POLICY FOR REQUIRING A CONFIRMATORY TRIAL TO BE UNDERWAY 112 PRIOR TO APPROVAL 113 9 FDA intends to address in other guidance complementary authorities added by the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023 to help ensure timely study completion. The Consolidated Appropriations Act authorizes FDA to specify the conditions for the progress of a required postapproval trial, which may include enrollment targets, the study protocol, and milestones, including the target date of study completion. See section 506(c)(2)(C) of the FD&C Act.

candidates.statement: Soon after sponsors and FDA reach preliminary alignment that a development program could 149 support accelerated approval, sponsors should request a meeting with FDA to discuss a 150 comprehensive drug development program, which includes plans for confirmatory trial(s), if 151 such plans are not already completed and agreed to. As soon as practicable, and generally soon 152 after the End-of-Phase 2 meeting, there should be agreement between FDA and the sponsor on 153 the design of the confirmatory trial(s) intended to verify and describe clinical benefit, including 154 FDA’s review of draft protocol(s). The trial must be feasible to conduct and appropriately 155 designed to verify and describe clinical benefit. 156
candidates.context: IV. UNDERWAY DETERMINATION 147 FDA generally intends to consider a confirmatory trial to be "underway" prior to accelerated 158 approval if (1) the trial has a target completion date that is consistent with diligent and timely 159 conduct of the trial, considering the nature of the trial’s design and objectives, (2) the sponsor’s 160 progress and plans for postapproval conduct of the trial provide sufficient assurance to expect 161 timely completion of the trial, and (3) enrollment of the confirmatory trial has been initiated. 162

candidates.statement: The timelines for the confirmatory trial – and in particular, the expected completion date – 170 should be discussed with FDA prior to the submission of the application for accelerated 171 approval. candidates.statement: Appropriate target completion dates may differ across therapeutic areas. In oncology, for 190 example, the median time from accelerated approval to verification of benefit is approximately 3 191 years (including FDA review) and has been decreasing over time. 12 Specific target completion 192 dates for a trial depend on more considerations than can be described here. In all cases, sponsors 193 should provide FDA with a clear and sound justification of the proposed target completion date 194 for the Agency’s consideration. 195

candidates.statement: The sponsor should propose benchmarks (including, e.g., participant recruitment goal, extent of 212 site activation, proportion of primary endpoint events accrued) consistent with the considerations 213 above that could be assessed at the time of the anticipated accelerated approval to facilitate 214 FDA's determination of whether the trial is underway. Benchmarks should be identified to allow 215 measurement of the sponsor’s progress, which if met would provide assurance of the trial’s 216 feasibility and allow the Agency to expect timely completion of the trial by an appropriate target 217 completion date. Sponsors should discuss with FDA whether the proposed benchmark(s) is/are 218 acceptable prior to submission of the application. Sponsors are expected to ensure adequate trial 219 resources such that implementation meets benchmark timelines. 220

candidates.statement: In planning the timeline for a confirmatory trial, sponsors should consider factors that may 237 adversely affect accrual, including how an accelerated approval and wider availability of the 238 drug are expected to impact the accrual and conduct of the confirmatory trial. For example, the 239 impact of an accelerated approval may be limited if the confirmatory trial is not being conducted 240 in the approved indication (e.g., the confirmatory trial is to be conducted in an earlier disease 241 stage or different treatment setting). Alternatively, the impact of approval may be greater if the 242 confirmatory trial is in the same population as the approved indication, particularly if the trial is 243 not at full or near full enrollment at the time of accelerated approval. In the latter setting, 244 sponsors should mitigate the anticipated impact of accelerated approval on participant enrollment 245 and retention by completing all or a significant portion of enrollment prior to accelerated 246 approval. Additionally, to ensure the confirmatory trial enrolls and retains sufficient U.S. 247 participants, the sponsor’s enrollment strategy should prioritize early U.S. recruitment, and U.S. 248 recruitment should be closer to completion at the time of accelerated approval. 249
